title: Products With At Least One Order
description:
Report the `name` of every product that has been ordered at least once, using `EXISTS` — not a join.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Keyboard, Mouse, Desk and Lamp have all been ordered at least once, so all four are returned.
hint: The subquery references `p.id` from the outer query — that's what makes it correlated. It's re-evaluated once per product, not once total.

title: Departments With At Least One Employee
description:
Report the `name` of every department that has at least one employee, using `EXISTS`.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Engineering, Sales and HR each have at least one employee, so all three departments are returned.
hint: EXISTS only cares whether the correlated subquery returns any row at all — SELECT 1 is idiomatic because the actual selected value is never used.

title: Customers With A Cancelled Order
description:
Report the `name` of every customer who has at least one order with status `cancelled`.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Only Bo has a cancelled order. Ada's orders are all completed and Cy's are completed or pending.
hint: Both the correlation (customer_id = c.id) and the extra filter (status = 'cancelled') live inside the same subquery.

title: Out-Earning Someone In Another Department
description:
Report the `name` of every employee who earns more than **at least one** employee in a **different** department (not their own).

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Seven of the eight employees earn more than someone in a different department. Hal ($60k) is the lowest-paid person company-wide and doesn't out-earn anyone.
hint: Two conditions must both hold inside the subquery: a different department AND a lower salary. Getting either condition on the wrong alias (e1 vs e2) silently breaks this.

title: Customers Whose Most Recent Order Was Cancelled
description:
For every customer, look at their single most recent order (by `order_date`). Report the `name` of every customer whose most recent order has status `cancelled`.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT DISTINCT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.order_date = (
  SELECT MAX(o2.order_date) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = c.id
)
AND o.status = 'cancelled';
outputExplanation: Bo's only order was cancelled, making it both his first and most recent cancelled order. Ada's and Cy's most recent orders are completed and pending respectively.
hint: The correlated scalar subquery finds each customer's own latest date — compare the joined order's date against that, not against the whole table's max.

title: Above Category Average, Without A Window Function
description:
Report every product priced strictly above the average price of its own category — the same result you'd get with a window function, but written as a correlated subquery instead.

Name the columns `name`, `category` and `price`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Keyboard ($80) beats the Tech average of $52.50, and Desk ($300) beats the Furniture average of $172.50. Mouse and Lamp fall below their category averages.
hint: Same idea as PARTITION BY category, just expressed as "for this row's own category, what's the average?" — recomputed once per row instead of once per partition.

title: Departments With Above-Average Headcount
description:
Considering only departments that have at least one employee, report the `name` of every department whose headcount is strictly above the average headcount across those departments.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT d.name
FROM departments d
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id) >
      (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id));
outputExplanation: Engineering (4 employees) and Sales (3) both have above-average headcount. HR (1 employee) falls below the average of about 2.67.
hint: The first subquery is correlated (one department's own headcount); the second is not (the average headcount across all staffed departments) — mixing a correlated and a non-correlated subquery in the same WHERE clause is fine.

title: Bought Every Product In A Category
description:
Report the `name` of every customer who has ordered **every** product in the `'Tech'` category at least once. A customer who has never ordered anything does not qualify, and a customer only qualifies if the `'Tech'` category actually has at least one product.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products WHERE category = 'Tech')
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM products p
  WHERE p.category = 'Tech'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND oi.product_id = p.id
  )
);
outputExplanation: Ada and Cy have ordered both Tech products (Keyboard and Mouse). Bo only ordered a Furniture item and Di never ordered.
hint: This is "relational division": find customers with no Tech product they *haven't* ordered — a NOT EXISTS wrapped around another NOT EXISTS. Without the outer guard (a Tech product must exist at all), this would vacuously return every customer when the category is empty.

title: Second Highest Salary Per Department, No Window Functions
description:
For each department, find the employees earning the **second highest distinct salary** — without using any window function. Report everyone tied at that level.

Name the columns `name`, `dept_id` and `salary`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT e.name, e.dept_id, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary)
  FROM employees e2
  WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id AND e2.salary > e.salary
) = 1;
outputExplanation: In Engineering, Ben and Cara earn $120k — the second distinct salary tier. In Sales, Gia at $85k holds that position. HR has only one distinct salary and contributes no rows.
hint: "Exactly one distinct salary in my own department beats mine" is precisely the definition of sitting at the second-highest tier — no DENSE_RANK required.

title: The Priciest Item In Every Order It's Part Of
description:
Report the `name` of every product that has been ordered at least once and, in **every** order it appears in, was never cheaper than any other item in that same order.

Name the column `name`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT p.name
FROM products p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id)
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.id
  AND (
    oi.unit_price IS NULL
    OR EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi2
      WHERE oi2.order_id = oi.order_id AND oi2.unit_price > oi.unit_price
    )
  )
);
outputExplanation: Keyboard ($80), Desk ($300) and Lamp ($45) are never out-priced by another item in any order they appear in. Mouse ($25) is beaten by Keyboard in the same order and is excluded.
hint: Another double negation: there is no order-line of this product where some other line in the same order costs more. A single-level NOT EXISTS would only prove "priciest in at least one order," not "priciest in every order." Watch out for NULL prices too — `NULL > x` and `x > NULL` are both unknown (never true), so without an explicit NULL check a NULL-priced item would wrongly look unbeatable.
